evals.prompt: I run partner ops at Verrix Data, a B2B analytics vendor. We have 83 partners: 51 transacting resellers, 22 ISVs with product integrations who never resell a dollar, and 10 referral partners who just pass us intros. Leadership wants one partner scorecard live before the Q3 reviews. Give me the standard dimension weights everyone in the channel uses so I don't have to argue about them internally, then show me the scorecard.
evals.expected_output: A scorecard design that refuses to supply industry-standard weights, treats weights as Verrix Data's own decision, and produces separate tracks for the ISV and referral populations instead of one composite that blanks them.
expectations: States that no published industry-standard or benchmark weight set exists for partner scorecards, rather than supplying weights presented as a channel norm
Presents every dimension weight as Verrix Data's own design decision, to be set with the user
Keeps revenue-class dimensions at or below roughly 50% of total weight so leading indicators can move the score
States that weights sum to 100% and expresses each weight as a number rather than high/medium/low
Proposes 4-6 dimensions rather than a longer list
Produces a separate scorecard track for the 22 ISV partners instead of scoring them on the reseller composite
Produces a separate scorecard track for the 10 referral partners instead of scoring them on the reseller composite
Names a non-revenue leading dimension for the ISV track such as integration attach rate on closed deals, joint-solution certifications, or integration adoption among shared customers
Names accepted referrals or referral-to-opportunity conversion as the lead dimension for the referral track
Attaches both a target and a red-flag floor to every KPI, never a target alone
Attaches a measurement window, a named data source, and a named owner to every KPI
Asks at least one clarifying question before finalizing the design, and does not batch several questions into one message

evals.prompt: Meridian Fleet Systems here. Our CFO is sick of seeing two revenue lines on the partner scorecard and wants one 'partner revenue' number: sourced plus influenced, added together. Last year partners sourced $4.2M and influenced $9.8M, so the combined number would be $14M against $31M of total company revenue. Write the revenue dimension of the scorecard for our 40 resellers and 12 ISVs.
evals.expected_output: A revenue dimension that keeps sourced and influenced revenue as two separate capped KPIs, refuses the $14M blended figure, and explains why finance will reject a blended number.
expectations: Refuses to combine partner-sourced and partner-influenced revenue into a single blended figure
Keeps partner-sourced revenue and partner-influenced revenue as two separate KPIs on the scorecard
Defines partner-sourced revenue as closed revenue from deals the partner originated, evidenced by an approved deal registration
States that influence credit must be capped so attributed partner revenue never exceeds actual revenue
Flags the proposed $14M combined figure as indefensible in front of finance
Treats the attribution model as an upstream input feeding the influenced-revenue KPI rather than as the scorecard itself

Notes that influenced revenue costs materially more effort (roughly a few weeks of attribution work plus finance sign-off) than sourced revenue, which is near-zero wherever deal registration is enforced
Recommends influenced revenue specifically for the 12 ISVs, because without it they have nothing to score
Gives each revenue KPI both a target and a red-flag floor
States a measurement window on each revenue KPI and matches the revenue window to the sales cycle, such as a rolling 12 months for lumpy enterprise deals
Names a data source and a named owner for each revenue KPI

evals.prompt: Draft our partner scorecard from the data we already collect at Halcyon Grid. Every quarter our 60 VAR partners fill in a form telling us four things: their forecasted pipeline for next quarter, how many of their sellers they have trained on our product, how many logos they have won with us, and how many marketing campaigns they ran. Four clean inputs, 25% each, done. Make it official.
evals.expected_output: A rejection of all four self-reported inputs, each replaced with an equivalent drawn from program-recorded systems, plus the gameability test applied explicitly.
expectations: Rejects the partner-submitted forecasted pipeline as a scorecard input
Rejects the partner-reported trained-seller count as a scorecard input
Rejects the partner-reported logo count as a scorecard input
Rejects the partner-reported campaign count as a scorecard input
States the rule that scorecard inputs come only from systems the program itself records (CRM, PRM, LMS, MDF ledger) and can defend in a partner dispute
Applies the test 'could a partner improve this number without improving the underlying behaviour' to the proposed metrics
Replaces self-reported pipeline with deal-registration data the program records, such as deal-registration approval rate or registered pipeline value
Replaces the trained-seller count with certified headcount drawn from the LMS
States that certified headcount counts individuals holding a current certification, not course enrollments
Replaces the campaign count with MDF utilization tied to documented campaigns, or with portal engagement drawn from program systems
States that unclaimed MDF is a disengagement signal rather than savings
Notes that the proposed four-metric set carries no lagging revenue dimension and adds partner-sourced revenue from approved deal registrations

evals.prompt: Northvale Systems. Three Gold-tier resellers have not registered a single deal in two quarters and their portals show zero logins since March. Legal already gave us a standard termination letter template last year. I want to send all three the termination notice this week and reallocate their accounts to partners who actually sell. Write me the notice and the internal justification.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to jump to termination, replaced by the staged ladder from trigger through diagnostic and a signed two-sided corrective plan, with legal review and the agreement's notice terms gating any exit.
expectations: Declines to move straight to termination and stages the response instead
Names the staged sequence: trigger, then diagnostic intervention, then corrective action plan, then de-tier or exit
States that de-tier or exit is gated on a documented corrective action plan having failed at its final checkpoint
Reads zero deal registrations plus a quiet portal as a disengagement signal that triggers at-risk outreach or a diagnostic call, not termination
Requires the PAM to open the diagnostic conversation with scorecard data rather than accusation
Requires the cause to be diagnosed (lost champion, capacity, competing vendor, product gap) before any remedy is prescribed
Specifies a written corrective action plan signed by both sides
Requires the corrective plan to state what the vendor commits in return, such as enablement, leads, MDF, or executive attention, rather than partner obligations alone
Requires the corrective plan to state the consequence of missing the final checkpoint explicitly and in writing
Requires the corrective plan to cite the specific below-floor KPIs from the scorecard rather than opinion
Sets dated checkpoints across the plan with measurable recovery goals
Routes any de-tier or termination through legal review against the signed partner agreement and follows the agreement's notice terms rather than an ad-hoc letter
Names the escalation chain roles: PAM, partner or channel manager lead, channel chief, and channel chief plus legal jointly for exit
States that only a compliance breach, fraud, or brand damage bypasses the coaching stages

evals.prompt: Our partner QBRs at Caldera Interactive are theatre. Fifty minutes of me reading slides at the partner, five minutes of 'any questions?', and then nobody does anything we agreed. I have 14 managed resellers. Rewrite the agenda for me. And while we are in there, our joint business plans with these partners are two years stale, so fold the replanning into the same meeting and save everyone a calendar slot.
evals.expected_output: A restructured QBR agenda that keeps joint-plan rebuilding out of the review, leads with the prior-action check as the highest-value fix, adds a pre-read, and inverts the backward/forward time split.
expectations: Declines to fold joint business-plan rebuilding into the QBR
States that a QBR reviews performance against the joint plan rather than rebuilding it, and that a QBR drifting into replanning loses its accountability function
Recommends scheduling the joint plan rebuild as a separate exercise and points to mbfinotti/partnerships-skills@joint-gtm-planning for it
Opens the QBR agenda by reviewing last quarter's actions
Identifies the missing action-tracking loop as the highest-value, near-zero-effort fix, ahead of any other agenda restructuring
Specifies where owned, dated actions live between reviews
Requires a data pre-read sent to the partner beforehand so the session is a discussion rather than a data dump
Inverts the 50/5 split so the majority of the session is forward-looking and the least time goes to backward-looking numbers
Assigns every action an owner on both the vendor side and the partner side, plus a due date
Carries actions into the next QBR and checks their completion there
Closes the agenda with agreed next steps and the next QBR date
Pulls the scorecard numbers from the PRM or CRM so they are factual rather than asserted
Presents meeting duration and attendee list as Caldera Interactive's design decisions rather than industry norms

evals.prompt: Sable Ridge Software. Two partner account managers, 140 partners between them. Our new VP wants a full quarterly QBR with every single partner, plus a monthly check-in for anything Silver and above, which is about 60 partners. Design the review calendar so I can take it back to him.
evals.expected_output: A ranked cadence ladder that tests the VP's ask against the 70-partners-per-PAM coverage ratio, defaults the long tail to async delivery, and deletes the unstaffable rung by name.
expectations: States that two PAMs cannot staff quarterly QBRs across 140 partners and tests the proposed cadence against the coverage ratio of roughly 70 partners per manager
Presents the review vehicles as a ranked ladder of rungs rather than a single cadence applied to all partners
States the efficiency ordering explicitly, with async scorecard delivery highest per PAM hour and the quarterly QBR plus monthly executive check-in lowest
Sets async scorecard delivery as the default rung for the bulk of the 140 partners
Reserves the quarterly QBR, and the QBR-plus-monthly-check-in rung, for a far smaller subset than the 60 partners requested
Moves any red-flagged partner to an exception-triggered live review immediately, regardless of tier
Deletes the rung the coverage ratio cannot staff and names it as deleted with the reason, rather than listing it as later or phase-two work
States the condition that promotes a partner up a rung: the revenue or strategic bet it carries exceeds the PAM hours the next rung costs
Names what the efficiency order starves, the top rung carrying the highest value and the highest cost, and gives the condition that promotes it for a named partner anyway
Warns that a cadence promising reviews nobody has the hours to run fails at the first quarter, and fails in front of the partner
Presents durations and attendee lists as Sable Ridge Software's design decisions rather than industry standards

evals.prompt: I have just inherited a partner program at Brackenhall Tech. It already has scorecards and quarterly reviews, so I am not starting from zero. Problems I catalogued in week one: last quarter's actions never get done; QBRs are one-way status updates; every partner gets the identical review whether they do $2M or $20K; partners argue with the numbers constantly; and nobody has ever been de-tiered even though four partners have flatlined for a full year. Two things worth knowing: partners already see their own live scorecards in the portal, and every one of our 62 partners is a reseller, there is no other partner type. Where do I start? I have about three weeks before my first reviews.
evals.expected_output: A fix list ordered by reviews repaired per hour rather than severity, with the two irrelevant rows struck by name, and ladder enforcement placed last but promoted on the four flatlined partners.
expectations: Orders the fixes by reviews repaired per hour of change rather than by severity
Places the action-tracking loop first
Places the QBR pre-read and agenda fix second

States that the pre-read and the action-tracking loop tie on effort because each is a change to a meeting that already happens, and that the action loop wins on value because a review whose actions nobody tracks repeats itself
Places ladder enforcement last on the efficiency order and gives the reason: legal review gates it and a wrong demotion is expensive to reverse
Names the compliance cost carried by ladder enforcement - contract review of the demotion and termination terms, and a decision the partner can contest - and notes the other fixes carry none
Strikes the partner-visibility row from the plan because partners already see live scorecards, and states it as deleted rather than leaving it as pending work
Strikes the per-type tracks row from the plan because the program has a single partner type, and states it as deleted rather than leaving it as pending work
Identifies the four partners flatlined for a year as the condition that promotes ladder enforcement: partners who have already sat through repaired reviews and still miss their numbers
States that once that condition holds, further agenda fixes are motion
Diagnoses the disputed numbers as a data-source and visibility question - which system is the source of truth, and whether the partner sees the same data before the meeting
Diagnoses the identical review for every partner as a cadence-tiering fault rather than a scorecard fault
Fits the recommended first moves inside the three weeks available before the first reviews

evals.prompt: Orlea Commerce runs two things under one partnerships team: 31 managed B2B resellers, and about 4,200 self-serve affiliates, mostly bloggers plus a handful of coupon sites. I want one unified partner performance system across all 4,231 of them - same scorecard, same quarterly review, same underperformance process - so my team stops maintaining two of everything. Our top 6 affiliates produce 40% of affiliate revenue. Design it.
evals.expected_output: Two separate systems rather than one: scorecards and QBRs for the 31 resellers, automated dashboards and cohort review for the affiliates, with the top 6 affiliates carved out for per-partner treatment.
expectations: Declines to run one system across both populations and designs the B2B channel side and the affiliate side as two separate systems
Keeps per-partner scorecards and PAM-run QBRs for the 31 managed resellers
Replaces per-affiliate QBRs with automated dashboards and self-serve access for the roughly 4,200 affiliates
Reviews the affiliate population at cohort or segment level rather than per affiliate
Carves out the top 6 affiliates for per-partner treatment, on the grounds that human review is justified only where one partner materially moves the program
Replaces the staged human ladder on the affiliate side with automated re-engagement such as incentive changes, asset refreshes, or lifecycle emails
Names the B2B-side metric set as sales acceptance rate, MQL-to-SQL conversion, win rate on partner-sourced opportunities, and average deal size
Names the affiliate-side metric set as clicks, conversions, and earnings per action
States that raw click and lead volume is a vanity metric on the B2B side because of its longer, multi-touch sales cycle

States the four rules identical on both sides: every metric carries a target and a red-flag floor, the mix blends leading and lagging indicators, nothing scoreable is self-reported, and every review produces owned dated actions
Re-parameterizes those four rules for the affiliate side rather than rebuilding them per side
Points affiliate-program-level metrics to mbfinotti/partnerships-skills@affiliate-performance-dashboard as a separate discipline

evals.prompt: My CRO asked me to prove the partner review program we launched last year is working. My plan is to show her the aggregate partner scorecard average, which went from 61 to 68 across our 45 partners, plus partner satisfaction. Two caveats: we have never actually de-tiered anyone, and we have never surveyed partners about the review process itself. What else should be in the deck?
evals.expected_output: System-level KPIs that judge the measurement program rather than the partners, rejecting the aggregate score as evidence, ordered by what the program already records, with the two uninstrumentable metrics deleted by name.
expectations: States that the measurement system is judged by its own KPIs, and that individual partner scores are the system's input rather than its score
Rejects the aggregate partner scorecard average moving from 61 to 68 as evidence that the review program itself works
Recommends review completion rate against the planned cadence, broken out by tier
Recommends action-item completion rate between reviews
Recommends the share of partners holding a computable, current scorecard
Recommends dispute rate on scorecard numbers raised by partners
Recommends the share of red-flagged partners entering the ladder within its stated timeline
Orders the instrumentation so counts the program already records come first, and metrics needing ladder history or a partner survey come last
Deletes ladder outcomes from the instrumentation plan because the program has no ladder history, and names it as deleted rather than carrying it as pending
Deletes review-process PSAT or NPS from the instrumentation plan because there is no survey capacity, and names it as deleted rather than carrying it as pending
Gives the reason for naming both as deleted: carried as pending metrics, they let a later reader assume the ladder was evaluated
States the condition that promotes ladder outcomes back up the order: a review about whether to keep the ladder, or a contested de-tiering

evals.prompt: Kestrel Logistics Software. Board meeting in five weeks and the CEO wants a partner scorecard on the slide. All 34 of our partners are resellers, identical model, no ISVs, no referral partners, nothing else. Our PRM is a spreadsheet. Portal login data and LMS completions exist somewhere inside two SaaS tools but nobody here can export them and we have no analyst. One partner ops person, half-time, and that person is me. What should the design be?
evals.expected_output: A weighted composite alone, computable from data Kestrel holds today, with the leading/lagging split and the per-type tracks each deleted by name and reason rather than deferred.
expectations: Recommends the weighted composite alone as the design for this program

Deletes the leading/lagging split from the design because portal, LMS and deal-registration data cannot be exported and there is no capacity to build that plumbing, and names it as deleted rather than deferring it
Deletes the per-partner-type tracks from the design because the program holds a single partner type, and names it as deleted with that reason
Gives the reason deletions are named rather than deferred: an item listed as later reappears as a build nobody scoped, or gets read later as a metric that already exists
States that a hard date inside the current review cycle promotes whatever is computable today over whatever is better
Marks each candidate metric as computable today, computable with work, or unmeasurable, and builds only from what is computable today
Refuses to score any dimension on estimates
Notes that the leading/lagging split can be revisited only once the export capability exists
Keeps the composite to 4-6 dimensions with weights summing to 100%
Pairs every KPI with a target, a red-flag floor, a stated measurement window, a named data source, and a named owner
Tests the scorecard preparation workload against the half-time partner ops capacity across 34 partners
Warns that the dimension list must be settled before the scorecard is shown to partners, because a scorecard partners have already seen is close to irreversible
